Algebra I · Lesson 5.1

Two Variables, Two Equations

Solve this lesson →All lessons

Here is a story one letter cannot carry. Lena scored 53 points on a quiz made of 2-point and 5-point questions, and she does not know the split. With aa correct 2-point answers and bb correct 5-point answers, her fact reads 2a+5b=532a+5b=53. No value of aa can be checked on its own. The claim involves both letters at once.

Problem
Four pairs are proposed for 2a+5b=532a+5b=53, each written with aa first and bb second. (24,1)(19,3)(9,7)(11,6)(24,1)(19,3)(9,7)(11,6) Substitute both values from each pair and evaluate the left side. Enter how many of the four pairs make the claim true.
Show a hint
  • Each pair gets the full check from 4.1. Replace aa and bb with the pair's two values, evaluate the left side, and compare it with 5353.
  • The last pair gives 2(11)+5(6)=22+302(11)+5(6)=22+30. Settle whether that is 5353, then run the other three the same way.
Show the full solution
The first three pairs pass, 48+5=5348+5=53, 38+15=5338+15=53, and 18+35=5318+35=53, while (11,6)(11,6) gives 22+30=5222+30=52. So 33​ of the four pairs make the claim true. Three different pairs already satisfy the same equation, and nothing in it stops more.
Key idea
A solution is a pair. An equation in two variables makes a claim about two numbers at once. A solution is a pair of values, one for each variable, that makes the claim true. Checking a candidate substitutes both values and evaluates each side, 4.1's check with two substitutions instead of one. The pair records which value belongs to which letter, so (24,1)(24,1) means a=24a=24 and b=1b=1, and the order matters. One number alone is not a solution, because the claim cannot even be tested until both letters have values.
Problem
The pair x=12, y=2x=12, y=2 solves 4x+9y=664x+9y=66, since 48+18=6648+18=66. Now swap the two values. Substitute x=2, y=12x=2, y=12 and enter the value the left side takes.
Show a hint
  • A pair says which value belongs to which letter, so the swapped version is a different pair making a different substitution.
  • With x=2x=2 and y=12y=12, the first term is 4(2)=84(2)=8 and the second is 9(12)9(12).
Show the full solution
With x=2x=2 and y=12y=12, the left side is 4(2)+9(12)=8+108=1164(2)+9(12)=8+108=116​. That is not 66, so the swapped pair fails. A pair carries its order, and (12,2)(12,2) and (2,12)(2,12) are different candidates.

Checking given pairs is one skill. Producing your own is the next. Choose a value for one variable and the equation collapses to one variable, which 4.2 solves. In Lena's equation, a=14a=14 gives 28+5b=5328+5b=53, so 5b=255b=25 and b=5b=5, the pair (14,5)(14,5). The story allows only whole counts, but the equation is its own object and takes any number.

Problem
The equation x+2y=49x+2y=49 has a solution pair with x=17x=17. Substitute that value, solve the equation that remains, and enter yy.
Show a hint
  • Substituting the given xx leaves an equation in yy alone, exactly the kind 4.2 solves.
  • After the substitution the claim reads 17+2y=4917+2y=49. Solve 2y=322y=32.
Show the full solution
Substituting x=17x=17 gives 17+2y=4917+2y=49, so 2y=322y=32 and y=16y=16​. The pair (17,16)(17,16) checks, 17+32=4917+32=49.
Problem
The equation 6x+y=426x+y=42 has a solution pair with x=10x=10. Substitute the given value, solve for the partner, and enter yy.
Show a hint
  • Replace xx with 1010 and compute 6x6x first. It is fine if that value comes out larger than 4242.
  • Substituting gives 60+y=4260+y=42. Since 6060 is already more than 4242, yy must be negative.
Show the full solution
Substituting x=10x=10 gives 60+y=4260+y=42, so y=42−60=−18y=42−60=−18​. The check passes, 60+(−18)=4260+(−18)=42. A solution pair can include a negative number.
Problem
The equation 3x+10y=583x+10y=58 has a solution pair with x=18x=18. Find the partner value and enter yy as a fraction in lowest terms.
Show a hint
  • The collapsed equation is 4.2 work, and nothing promises a whole-number answer.
  • Substituting gives 54+10y=5854+10y=58. Solve 10y=410y=4, then reduce.
Show the full solution
Substituting x=18x=18 gives 54+10y=5854+10y=58, so 10y=410y=4 and y=410=25y=104​=52​​. Nothing restricts pairs to whole numbers. Every choice of xx, whole or not, gets a partner.
Key idea
One equation, many solutions. Every value chosen for xx collapses a two-variable equation into a one-variable equation, and 4.2 finds the partner yy. A different xx gives a different pair, so the supply of solutions never runs out, and the pairs come whole, negative, and fractional. The consequence is that one equation in two variables cannot pin down its pair. Solving it cannot mean finding the solution, because there is no single solution to find.
Fun fact
Around 250 CE, Diophantus of Alexandria filled his Arithmetica with problems that have more unknowns than equations, so endless solutions fit. He was content to find one. Equations like these are still called Diophantine in his honor.

Two secret numbers satisfy x+y=101x+y=101. Finding them looks hopeless, since pairs passing that test can be listed all day and every one of them keeps the secret. Suppose a second fact about the same two numbers turns up. It is worth asking what one more fact could possibly change.

Problem
All four of these pairs satisfy x+y=101x+y=101. (98,3)(93,8)(79,22)(70,31)(98,3)(93,8)(79,22)(70,31) Now the second fact arrives. The same two numbers also satisfy x−y=39x−y=39. Enter how many of the four pairs satisfy both facts.
Show a hint
  • Each pair already passes the first fact, so only the new claim needs testing.
  • The first pair gives 98−3=9598−3=95, not 3939. Keep going down the list.
Show the full solution
The differences are 98−3=9598−3=95, 93−8=8593−8=85, 79−22=5779−22=57, and 70−31=3970−31=39. Only (70,31)(70,31) gives 3939, so 11​ pair satisfies both facts. The first fact allowed an endless list, and the second fact cut it to one pair.
Key idea
A system of equations. A set of equations about the same variables, all required to hold at once, is called a system of equations. A solution of a system is a pair that satisfies every equation in it, and a pair that fails even one equation is not a solution, no matter how many of the others it satisfies. This is why a second equation has power. Each equation alone allows endless pairs, but few pairs pass every test, and often the count is exactly one.

Lena knew one more fact all along. The quiz had 13 questions, so a+b=13a+b=13 must also hold. Of every pair passing 2a+5b=532a+5b=53, only (4,9)(4,9) passes both, since 8+45=538+45=53 and 4+9=134+9=13. She got four 2-point questions and nine 5-point questions. Checking a pair against a system means checking it against every equation in it.

Problem
For the system 2u+v=692u+v=69 and u+v=37u+v=37, test the pairs (30,9)(30,9), (32,5)(32,5), and (26,11)(26,11). One satisfies only the first equation, one satisfies only the second, and one satisfies both. Enter uu for the solution of the system.
Show a hint
  • A solution of a system passes every equation in it. A pair that fails one check is not a solution, even if it passes every other.
  • (30,9)(30,9) makes the first equation true, since 60+9=6960+9=69. Check it in the second before deciding anything.
Show the full solution
(30,9)(30,9) gives 60+9=6960+9=69 but 30+9=3930+9=39, not 3737. (26,11)(26,11) gives 26+11=3726+11=37 but 52+11=6352+11=63, not 6969. (32,5)(32,5) gives 64+5=6964+5=69 and 32+5=3732+5=37, so it passes both and u=32u=32​. Each rejected pair passed exactly one equation, and one pass is worth nothing in a system.
Problem
Both (13,7)(13,7) and (29,3)(29,3) satisfy x+4y=41x+4y=41. Only one of them also satisfies 2x−y=192x−y=19. Enter x+yx+y for the solution of the system.
Show a hint
  • Passing the first equation is not enough. Run each pair through the second and keep the one that passes.
  • For (29,3)(29,3), the left side of the second equation is 58−358−3. Compare that with 1919.
Show the full solution
For (29,3)(29,3), 2x−y=58−3=552x−y=58−3=55, not 1919. For (13,7)(13,7), 2x−y=26−7=192x−y=26−7=19, and 13+28=4113+28=41 confirms the first. The solution is (13,7)(13,7), so x+y=13+7=20x+y=13+7=20​.

How is that single pair found when no candidates are given? For now, by search. Take the friendlier equation, list whole-number pairs that satisfy it, and test each one in the other equation until a pair passes both. This works when the numbers are kind, and it fails the moment they are not. Lessons 5.2 and 5.3 build methods that always work.

Problem
Two numbers satisfy x+y=23x+y=23 and 5x−y=255x−y=25. List whole-number pairs from the first equation and test them in the second until one passes. Enter xx.
Show a hint
  • Every candidate from the first fact has the form xx and 23−x23−x, so each choice of xx names a full pair to test.
  • If a test comes out below 2525, raise xx and try again. The value of 5x−y5x−y climbs quickly as xx grows, so the search stays short.
Show the full solution
Candidates from the first equation include (7,16)(7,16), (8,15)(8,15), and (9,14)(9,14). Testing (8,15)(8,15) in the second, 5(8)−15=40−15=255(8)−15=40−15=25, so both facts hold and x=8x=8​. Raising xx by 11 raises 5x−y5x−y by 66, so the second equation is hit exactly once.
Problem
The system m+n=67m+n=67 and m+n=73m+n=73 makes two claims about the same two numbers. Take any pair satisfying the first equation, test it in the second, and enter the number of solutions of the system.
Show a hint
  • Read the two claims side by side. Both are about the sum of the same two numbers.
  • A pair with m+n=67m+n=67 makes the second left side 6767, and 6767 is not 7373.
Show the full solution
Any pair passing the first equation has m+n=67m+n=67, so in the second equation its left side is 6767, never 7373. No pair passes both, and the system has 00​ solutions. Two claims about the same numbers can simply contradict each other. Chapter 7 will draw what that looks like.
Key idea
What a system can have. Usually a second fact pins the pair down and the system has exactly one solution. Sometimes the two claims conflict, as m+n=67m+n=67 and m+n=73m+n=73 do, and the system has no solution at all. Testing settles any pair somebody names, but it cannot produce a pair from nothing, and searching works only while the numbers are kind. Closing that gap, finding the pair instead of confirming it, is this chapter's work.
Problem
Two numbers satisfy x+y=6x+y=6 and x−y=14x−y=14. Search pairs from the first fact, and do not stop at positive candidates. Enter yy.
Show a hint
  • The difference 1414 is larger than the sum 66. Two positive numbers always differ by less than their sum, so one member must be negative.
  • Pairs summing to 6 include ones with a negative member, like 99 and −3−3.
Show the full solution
Pairs from the first fact run (7,−1)(7,−1), (8,−2)(8,−2), (9,−3)(9,−3), (10,−4)(10,−4). Testing (10,−4)(10,−4) in the second, 10−(−4)=1410−(−4)=14, so both facts hold and y=−4y=−4​. Positive pairs summing to 66 differ by less than 66, so the pair that works has to include a negative member.

A system is two claims sharing one pair. Testing confirms a pair, and searching finds one while the numbers stay kind, but they will not stay kind. Lesson 5.2, Substitution, turns two equations in two variables into one equation in one variable, chapter 4's home ground.

Practice these ideas

Practice
Substitute the pair x=11, y=2x=11, y=2 into 8x+3y=948x+3y=94 and evaluate the left side. It matches the right side. Enter the number both sides equal.
Show the solution
The left side is 8(11)+3(2)=88+6=948(11)+3(2)=88+6=94​. One check settles a pair, both values go in together and the two sides are compared once.
Practice
The pair (7,6)(7,6) is claimed to solve 9x+4y=919x+4y=91. Substitute x=7, y=6x=7, y=6 and enter the value the left side actually takes.
Show the solution
9(7)+4(6)=63+24=879(7)+4(6)=63+24=87​. That is not 9191, so (7,6)(7,6) is not a solution. A check either matches the right side or it does not, and this one misses by 44.
Practice
The equation 7x+y=867x+y=86 has a solution pair with x=11x=11. Substitute that value and solve for the letter that remains. Enter yy.
Show the solution
Substituting x=11x=11 gives 77+y=8677+y=86, so y=9y=9​. Check, 7(11)+9=77+9=867(11)+9=77+9=86, and the pair (11,9)(11,9) passes.
Practice
The equation x−2y=11x−2y=11 has a solution pair with y=12y=12. Enter xx.
Show the solution
Substituting y=12y=12 gives x−24=11x−24=11, so x=35x=35​. Check, 35−2(12)=35−24=1135−2(12)=35−24=11. Either member of the pair can be the given one.
Practice
Check the pairs (6,0)(6,0), (4,6)(4,6), (3,8)(3,8), (5,2)(5,2) against 3x+y=183x+y=18, substituting xx first and yy second. Enter how many of the four are solutions.
Show the solution
The left sides are 18+0=1818+0=18, 12+6=1812+6=18, 9+8=179+8=17, 15+2=1715+2=17, so 22​ of the pairs are solutions. Zero is a legal value for a member of a pair, and (6,0)(6,0) passes like any other.
Practice
Substitute the pair (24,9)(24,9) into x+9y=4x+yx+9y=4x+y, evaluating each side separately. Both sides come out to the same number. Enter it.
Show the solution
The left side is 24+81=10524+81=105 and the right side is 96+9=10596+9=105, so both sides equal 105105​. The pair checks against the whole claim at once, whichever side each letter appears on.
Practice
The equation 8x+y=508x+y=50 has a solution pair with x=9x=9. Enter yy.
Show the solution
Substituting x=9x=9 gives 72+y=5072+y=50, so y=50−72=−22y=50−72=−22​. Check, 8(9)+(−22)=72−22=508(9)+(−22)=72−22=50. The pair has a negative member, and the check passes all the same.
Practice
The equation 8x+6y=858x+6y=85 has a solution pair with x=8x=8. Enter yy as a fraction in lowest terms.
Show the solution
Substituting x=8x=8 gives 64+6y=8564+6y=85, so 6y=216y=21 and y=216=72y=621​=27​​. Check, 64+6⋅72=64+21=8564+6⋅27​=64+21=85. Nothing in the equation forces yy to be a whole number.
Practice
The equation 4y−3x=214y−3x=21 has a solution pair with x=9x=9. Enter yy.
Show the solution
Substituting x=9x=9 gives 4y−27=214y−27=21, so 4y=484y=48 and y=12y=12​. Check, 4(12)−3(9)=48−27=214(12)−3(9)=48−27=21.
Practice
Every pair solving x+5y=88x+5y=88 also solves 3x+15y=2643x+15y=264, since the second equation is the first with both sides multiplied by 33. The second fact adds nothing new. Enter yy for the pair with x=13x=13.
Show the solution
Using the first equation, 13+5y=8813+5y=88, so 5y=755y=75 and y=15y=15​. Check in the second, 3(13)+15(15)=39+225=2643(13)+15(15)=39+225=264. A second equation only pins the pair when it says something the first did not.
Practice
All four of (35,11)(35,11), (37,7)(37,7), (39,3)(39,3), (28,25)(28,25) satisfy 2x+y=812x+y=81. Exactly one also satisfies 3x−y=1043x−y=104. Enter xx for that pair.
Show the solution
Testing the second equation, 105−11=94105−11=94, 111−7=104111−7=104, 117−3=114117−3=114, 84−25=5984−25=59. Only (37,7)(37,7) passes both, so x=37x=37​. A solution of a system must satisfy every equation, and failing even one rules a pair out.
Practice
Two numbers add to 8787 and differ by 3333. Enter the larger number.
Show the solution
The facts are x+y=87x+y=87 and x−y=33x−y=33. Searching pairs that sum to 8787, the pair (60,27)(60,27) gives 60−27=3360−27=33, so the larger number is 6060​. Check, 60+27=8760+27=87.
Practice
Two numbers satisfy x+y=29x+y=29 and 4x+y=714x+y=71. Test whole-number pairs from the first equation in the second until one passes, then enter the product xyxy.
Show the solution
The pair (14,15)(14,15) sums to 2929, and 4(14)+15=56+15=714(14)+15=56+15=71 passes the second equation. So xy=14⋅15=210xy=14⋅15=210​. No other whole pair works, since raising xx by 11 raises 4x+y4x+y by 33, so 7171 is hit exactly once.
Practice
For the system x+y=102x+y=102 and x+y=89x+y=89, any pair satisfying the first equation misses the second by one fixed amount. Enter that amount.
Show the solution
Any pair with x+y=102x+y=102 makes the second equation read 102=89102=89, which misses by 102−89=13102−89=13​. The two claims conflict for every pair at once, so this system has no solution.
Practice
The system x+y=112x+y=112 and x−y=112x−y=112 looks like the impossible kind, but the left sides differ, and it has exactly one solution. Enter xx.
Show the solution
If adding yy and subtracting yy leave the same value, then y=0y=0, and the first equation gives x=112x=112​. Check, 112+0=112112+0=112 and 112−0=112112−0=112. Zero is a legal member of a pair, so the two claims agree instead of conflicting.
Practice
Two numbers satisfy m+n=5m+n=5 and m−n=17m−n=17. Search pairs from the first fact, and let the second number go negative. Enter nn.
Show the solution
The pair (11,−6)(11,−6) gives 11+(−6)=511+(−6)=5 and 11−(−6)=11+6=1711−(−6)=11+6=17, so n=−6n=−6​. A search that stops at positive candidates never finds this pair, since positive pairs summing to 55 differ by at most 55.
Practice
For one particular number kk, the pair x=16, y=−9x=16, y=−9 is the solution of the system x+y=7x+y=7 and 2x+5y=k2x+5y=k. Enter kk.
Show the solution
The first equation checks, 16+(−9)=716+(−9)=7. Substituting the pair into the second, k=2(16)+5(−9)=32−45=−13k=2(16)+5(−9)=32−45=−13​. Keep the parentheses, 5(−9)5(−9) is −45−45, and the term joins the sum with its sign.
